Pregnancy

Unexpected pregnancy symptoms: nosebleeds, discharge, sleep and digestion

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Nausea and backache are familiar pregnancy topics, but a blocked nose, more discharge, sleeplessness or extra gas can be unexpected. These changes can happen during an established pregnancy without meaning that everyone will experience them. You can ask about them without embarrassment, and being common does not mean a symptom should always be dismissed.

A symptom is a clue, not a pregnancy test

Hormonal changes, increased circulation and changes in digestion can affect parts of the body far from the uterus. The pattern differs between people and across pregnancy. Having none of these symptoms does not by itself signal a problem, and having several does not confirm pregnancy or show whether a baby is well.

If pregnancy has not been confirmed, use an appropriately timed pregnancy test and seek clinical advice when needed. Once pregnant, describe what changed, when it started, its severity and any accompanying symptoms. A new, persistent or worsening problem may have a cause other than pregnancy, even if someone else had a similar experience.

A blocked nose or a nosebleed can happen

Pregnancy-related hormonal and circulation changes can make the delicate nasal lining more congested and prone to bleeding. Dry air, forceful blowing, allergies, infection, injury or medicines can also contribute. Pregnancy is not an explanation for every nosebleed. Tell your clinician about repeated bleeding, blood-thinning medicines or a known clotting problem.

For mild congestion or dryness, a ready-made saline spray or gel and a properly maintained humidifier may help. Avoid picking or forcefully blowing the nose. Check any medicated nasal product with a pharmacist or maternity clinician rather than assuming an over-the-counter or natural remedy is suitable. If using a nasal-rinse device, use only distilled, sterile, or properly boiled-and-cooled water, and follow its cleaning instructions; untreated tap water is not appropriate for nasal irrigation.

Know what to do during a nosebleed

Sit upright and lean forward with your mouth open. Pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils continuously for 10–15 minutes and breathe through your mouth; use a clock rather than repeatedly letting go to check. Do not tilt your head back or lie flat. Spit out blood that reaches your mouth rather than swallowing it.

Get emergency assessment if bleeding lasts beyond 10–15 minutes, seems excessive, makes you vomit after swallowing a lot of blood, follows a head injury, or occurs with weakness, dizziness or breathing difficulty. Do not wait out the timing if one of those other signs is present. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. After it stops, avoid blowing or picking the nose, hot drinks and strenuous activity for 24 hours. Seek immediate medical care for headache, fever, confusion or vomiting after nasal rinsing.

More vaginal discharge needs context

More discharge is common in pregnancy and can increase further toward birth. Healthy discharge is usually thin, clear or milky white without an unpleasant smell. If a plain, unscented liner helps comfort, change it when damp and stop using it if it irritates. Avoid douching or perfumed intimate products; do not put a tampon in to manage discharge.

Contact your maternity clinician for unpleasant or unusual odour, green or yellow discharge, itching, soreness or pain when passing urine. These may need testing and pregnancy-appropriate treatment rather than a guessed infection remedy. Any vaginal bleeding needs immediate maternity advice. A watery trickle or gush may be amniotic fluid: contact maternity care immediately, even if there is no pain or the leak is small. Use a pad, not a tampon, and do not wait until the next day to see whether it continues.

You can feel tired and still struggle to sleep

Insomnia can mean trouble falling asleep, repeated waking or being unable to return to sleep. It may occur with or without obvious tiredness, at different stages of pregnancy, or not at all. Discomfort, reflux, needing the toilet, anxiety and other conditions can contribute. There is no promise that every sleep problem will simply pass or that you must endure it until birth.

Try a regular sleep-and-wake routine, a calm wind-down, less late caffeine and suitable daytime activity. Adjust long or late naps if they interfere with night sleep, while allowing needed rest. From 28 weeks, go to sleep on either side; if you wake on your back, turn onto your side. Ask for help when poor sleep affects daily life, or with persistent low mood, loss of interest, loud snoring or breathing pauses. Behavioural treatment can help; check any sleep medicine or supplement with your clinician rather than self-starting it.

Bloating, belching and passing wind

Gas can come from swallowed air and bacteria breaking down food in the bowel. Pregnancy-related slowing of digestion and constipation can add to discomfort; this is not the intestine literally twisting or turning over. Belching, bloating and passing wind are bodily functions, and you do not need to apologise for discussing them with your care team.

Smaller meals, eating slowly, fewer fizzy drinks and gentle activity may help. Notice your own triggers without cutting out whole nutritious food groups on someone else's advice. Allow toilet breaks and privacy rather than holding stool because of embarrassment. If gas symptoms keep bothering you, change suddenly or accompany pain, vomiting, bowel changes or weight loss, ask for assessment rather than assuming they are harmless pregnancy gas.

Constipation deserves relief, not blame

Pregnancy hormones can slow bowel movement. Stools may become hard or difficult to pass, less frequent, or leave a feeling of incomplete emptying. Some medicines and iron supplements can contribute. Increase fibre gradually through suitable foods, drink regularly enough to stay hydrated and keep appropriate movement; follow any individual fluid or activity restrictions. Respond to the urge to open your bowels rather than repeatedly delaying it.

If these steps do not help, ask a pharmacist, midwife or doctor about a suitable laxative and how to use it. Do not stop prescribed iron or other treatment on your own; an alternative may be possible. Persistent painful constipation, blood in stool or a new bowel change needs review. Bloating with vomiting, fever or inability to pass urine, stool or wind needs urgent assessment; severe pain belongs in the emergency group below, not in a longer trial of fibre.

Make asking for help easier

A short note can help: the symptom, timing, frequency, what makes it better or worse, medicines and what you have tried. For discharge, mention colour, smell, irritation, blood or watery leakage; for nosebleeds, duration and approximate amount; for sleep or bowel problems, how daily life is affected. You can ask to speak privately or write a question down if saying it aloud is difficult.

A friend or relative may offer useful practical support and help you feel less alone. Their experience cannot diagnose your symptom or prove a remedy safe or effective. Feeling worried is not a personal failing, and needing treatment is not a failure to cope. Ask your maternity team which changes to report, how to get advice outside office hours and when to arrange a review.

Do not label warning signs as just another symptom

Contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, suspected fluid leakage, regular contractions or tightenings before 37 weeks, or reduced baby movements once you normally feel them. Seek prompt assessment for fever, painful urination, ongoing abdominal pain or worsening symptoms; severe headache or visual changes also need immediate maternity advice. A persistent symptom affecting eating, sleep or bowel function deserves help even without an emergency sign.

Get emergency help for heavy vaginal bleeding on its own; severe or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain; pain in that area provoked by movement or touch; or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion. Vaginal bleeding with shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help, even without pelvic pain or heavy bleeding. Do not drive yourself: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Use the nosebleed emergency criteria above too. You do not need every warning sign, a sudden onset or a positive pregnancy test before seeking urgent help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Describe the actual change and its effect on daily life; ask privately if that makes discussion easier. Do not use symptoms as a pregnancy test or proof that everything is well.

Use correct nosebleed first aid and safe nasal-rinse water, and ask a clinician about abnormal discharge, persistent sleep problems or constipation treatment.

Keep maternity and emergency contact routes available. Report bleeding or watery leakage immediately and use emergency care for the independent warning signs rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise symptom dates, nosebleed duration, sleep and bowel observations, medicines and questions for your maternity team. It cannot confirm pregnancy, assess blood loss, distinguish vaginal discharge from amniotic fluid, diagnose an infection or replace examination. Recording symptoms must not delay urgent or emergency care.

When to seek help

Any pregnancy bleeding or possible fluid leak needs immediate maternity contact. Heavy vaginal bleeding, severe/worsening or movement/touch-provoked abdominal or pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion needs emergency help. A nosebleed lasting beyond 10–15 minutes or with excessive bleeding, swallowed blood causing vomiting, head injury, weakness, dizziness or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Vaginal bleeding with shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help, even without pelvic pain or heavy bleeding. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not use untreated tap water for nasal rinsing or start pregnancy medicines on peer advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Nose, discharge, sleep and digestive changes can occur, but no checklist confirms pregnancy or guarantees wellbeing.
  • For a nosebleed, lean forward and pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes; persistent or heavy bleeding and associated symptoms need emergency assessment.
  • Only suitable water belongs in a nasal-rinse device; a small watery vaginal leak or any vaginal bleeding needs immediate maternity advice.
  • Sleep, gas and constipation problems deserve practical support and clinician-selected treatment when needed.
  • Seek emergency help for severe or worsening pain or heavy vaginal bleeding; do not drive yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Is a nosebleed in pregnancy always harmless?

No. It can be common, but recurrent bleeding needs review. Lean forward and pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes. Bleeding beyond that, excessive blood, blood-swallowing with vomiting, head injury, weakness, dizziness or breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment without waiting for all signs.

Can I rinse my nose with ordinary tap water?

No. Use distilled, sterile or properly boiled-and-cooled water and follow the device's cleaning instructions. A ready-made saline spray may be simpler. Get immediate medical care for headache, fever, confusion or vomiting after nasal rinsing.

Is extra vaginal discharge normal?

Thin, clear or milky discharge without an unpleasant smell can be normal. New odour, green/yellow colour, itch, soreness or painful urination needs clinical advice. Any bleeding or a watery trickle/gush needs immediate maternity contact; do not assume all wetness is ordinary discharge.

Can insomnia happen even when I feel exhausted?

Yes. Trouble falling or staying asleep can coexist with tiredness. A routine, relaxation, less late caffeine and suitable activity may help, but persistent impairment or mood symptoms deserves care. Do not assume sleep medicines or supplements are suitable without advice.

Is a lot of gas in pregnancy always normal?

Gas and belching can occur, but persistent, changed or painful symptoms need assessment. Try slower, smaller meals and gentle movement. Vomiting, fever, inability to pass stool or wind, or severe pain should not be treated as routine gas.

What can I do about constipation?

Try gradually increasing suitable fibre, regular fluids and appropriate activity. If this is not enough, ask a pharmacist or maternity clinician about treatment. Do not stop prescribed iron yourself, and seek help for pain, bleeding or a persistent change.

Should I just copy a remedy that helped someone else?

Their support may be valuable, but their experience does not establish your diagnosis or a remedy's pregnancy safety. Check medicines, supplements and persistent symptoms with your care team. You can ask privately or bring written questions.

Which symptoms mean I should not wait?

Contact maternity care immediately for bleeding, possible waters breaking or reduced movements. Emergency help is needed for heavy vaginal bleeding, severe/worsening or movement/touch-provoked abdominal or pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion. Follow the nosebleed emergency criteria too. Vaginal bleeding with shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help, even without pelvic pain or heavy bleeding. Do not drive yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
